purpose: Rendered visual placement inventory; qualitative teaching decisions are recorded separately.

figures.heading: Why are these things made from different materials?
figures.alt: Examples of everyday products connected to chemistry.
figures.title: Chemistry is already part of your day
figures.caption: Electronics, fibres, medicines, food, clean water, fertilizers, cleaning products and outdoor equipment all depend on material properties and chemical processes.Original course illustration generated for Science 24.

figures.heading: From small units to useful products
figures.alt: Illustrative close-up: water beads on dark rain-jacket fabric at left, while a cream towel absorbs water at right.
figures.title: Same kind of molecule, different jobs
figures.caption: A rain shell sheds water; a cotton towel absorbs it. Both can be made of polymers, but their molecules and fabric structures give them different useful properties. Illustrative image; the molecular chains are not shown.

figures.heading: Read the symbol, the words and the instructions
figures.alt: Household hazardous product flammable symbol: black flame inside an octagon.
figures.title: Two flame symbols, two label systems
figures.caption: A symbol alerts you to a hazard; it does not identify an unknown product or give every handling instruction. Official examples: Health Canada household symbols and CCOHS WHMIS pictograms.

figures.heading: Read the symbol, the words and the instructions
figures.alt: Historical WHMIS symbol panel from the supplied Unit A textbook.
figures.title: Read the hazard before you handle the product
figures.caption: The supplied textbook uses the WHMIS symbols from its publication era. The lesson connects that historical source to current SDS terminology and modern workplace hazard communication.Source: supplied Science 24 Unit A textbook, printed p. 19.

figures.heading: Follow matter across the reaction arrow
figures.alt: Methane and oxygen are reactants; the arrow leads to carbon dioxide and water as products.
figures.title: Follow the reaction arrow
figures.caption: Methane and oxygen are reactants; the arrow leads to carbon dioxide and water as products. Conceptual schematic, not to scale.

figures.heading: What counts as useful evidence?
figures.alt: Textbook drawings show five observations: colour change, odour, a new solid, bubbles and energy transfer.
figures.title: Look for clues; test the explanation
figures.caption: Science 24 textbook, printed p. 34 (PDF p. 26), Figure 2.10. These are clues to investigate, not proof on their own. Use the table above to consider another explanation before deciding that a new substance formed.

figures.heading: Why can a reaction warm your hand?
figures.alt: Comparison of exothermic and endothermic reaction energy changes.
figures.title: Follow the direction of energy transfer
figures.caption: Exothermic reactions transfer energy from the reacting system to the surroundings overall. Endothermic reactions take in energy overall.Original course illustration generated for Science 24.

figures.heading: Four useful patterns
figures.alt: Textbook page explaining simple composition, decomposition and other reaction types.
figures.title: Reaction patterns from the source textbook
figures.caption: Use the pattern of reactants and products—not the colour of the substances or whether the equation looks complicated—to classify a reaction.Source: supplied Science 24 Unit A textbook, printed p. 44.

figures.alt: In 3H₂O, the coefficient 3 counts whole molecules and the subscript 2 counts hydrogen atoms per molecule.
figures.title: Read a coefficient and a subscript
figures.caption: In 3H₂O, the coefficient 3 counts whole molecules and the subscript 2 counts hydrogen atoms per molecule. Conceptual schematic, not to scale.

figures.alt: Balanced water formation: four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side.
figures.title: Conserve each kind of atom
figures.caption: Balanced water formation: four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side. Conceptual schematic, not to scale.

figures.heading: Track carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and energy
figures.alt: Textbook page about fossil fuel combustion.
figures.title: Combustion connects chemistry to energy use
figures.caption: The textbook follows fossil fuels from their chemical composition through combustion. The online lesson adds the atom-tracking and evidence students need to interpret the reaction.Source: supplied Science 24 Unit A textbook, printed p. 60.

figures.heading: Trace the energy in the right order
figures.alt: Sunlight supplies energy to the surface. Infrared radiation is absorbed and emitted by greenhouse gases; some energy still escapes to space.
figures.title: Energy enters and energy still leaves
figures.caption: Sunlight supplies energy to the surface. Infrared radiation is absorbed and emitted by greenhouse gases; some energy still escapes to space. Conceptual schematic, not to scale.

figures.heading: Use pH to describe the water—not to name the acid
figures.alt: Textbook page introducing acid-base reactions.
figures.title: Acid–base reactions in the source material
figures.caption: Use pH and reaction evidence to reason about acidity and neutralization. Do not treat pH as a substance name or a colour chart to memorize without meaning.Source: supplied Science 24 Unit A textbook, printed p. 66.

figures.heading: Three source-based approaches
figures.alt: Textbook air-pollution diagram showing formation of acid deposition.
figures.title: Trace pollutants through the atmosphere
figures.caption: The source diagram links sulfur- and nitrogen-containing emissions to acidic products and deposition. Follow which substance changes at each stage.Source: supplied Science 24 Unit A textbook, printed p. 64.

figures.heading: Why does a scratch matter?
figures.alt: Rusting steel beside barrier coating, galvanized zinc and sacrificial protection examples.
figures.title: Corrosion and three ways to protect steel
figures.caption: Rusting requires access to oxygen and water. Barrier coatings reduce contact; zinc and sacrificial metals add another protection mechanism.Original course illustration generated for Science 24.

figures.heading: Protect the metal by interrupting the process
figures.alt: A scratch in a barrier coating exposes iron to oxygen and water.
figures.title: A gap changes what reaches the iron
figures.caption: A scratch in a barrier coating exposes iron to oxygen and water. Conceptual schematic, not to scale.

figures.heading: Input → converter → outputs
figures.alt: Electrical input enters a fan motor; moving air is useful while heat and sound are other outputs.
figures.title: Follow input, converter and outputs
figures.caption: Electrical input enters a fan motor; moving air is useful while heat and sound are other outputs. Conceptual schematic; not to scale.

figures.heading: Read the textbook generator diagram
figures.alt: Two textbook diagrams. Kinetic input passes through a generator to electrical output; moving a wire loop through a magnetic field produces current.
figures.caption: Science 24 textbook, printed p. 101 (PDF p. 16). The full page remains available in Textbook Practice.

figures.heading: Movement and magnetic field change
figures.alt: A turbine turns a shaft; relative motion between a magnet and coil produces electrical output in a circuit.
figures.title: Separate turbine and generator
figures.caption: A turbine turns a shaft; relative motion between a magnet and coil produces electrical output in a circuit. Conceptual schematic; not to scale.

figures.heading: Trace each pathway
figures.alt: Cutaway of a hydroelectric machine. Lower turbine B receives water at arrow 5; wicket gates 3 guide it onto blades 4. Shaft 6 connects the turbine to generator A above, where rotor 2 turns within stator 1.
figures.title: Inside a hydroelectric turbine
figures.caption: Water enters the lower turbine (B) at arrow 5 and turns its blades (4). The shared shaft (6) turns the generator (A) above. Adjustable gates (3) control the water flow. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers illustration, public domain; identified through the CBE Science 24 Unit B lesson.

figures.heading: Efficiency = useful ÷ input × 100%
figures.alt: One hundred joules enters a device; thirty joules becomes useful light and seventy joules becomes other outputs.
figures.title: Account for useful and other outputs
figures.caption: One hundred joules enters a device; thirty joules becomes useful light and seventy joules becomes other outputs. Conceptual schematic; not to scale.

figures.heading: Read the word equation as a process
figures.alt: Light, carbon dioxide and water support glucose formation in chloroplasts; mitochondria use fuel and oxygen for cell work.
figures.title: Compare plant energy processes
figures.caption: Light, carbon dioxide and water support glucose formation in chloroplasts; mitochondria use fuel and oxygen for cell work. Conceptual schematic; not to scale.

figures.heading: Label the levels correctly
figures.alt: Four levels: grass producer, grasshopper primary consumer, frog secondary consumer and hawk tertiary consumer.
figures.title: Name four trophic levels
figures.caption: Four levels: grass producer, grasshopper primary consumer, frog secondary consumer and hawk tertiary consumer. Conceptual schematic; not to scale.

figures.heading: A coal formation sequence
figures.alt: Four textbook drawings labelled A to D show wetland plants, buried organic matter, increasing sediment layers and a coal seam deep below the surface.
figures.title: Follow the layers from A to D
figures.caption: Science 24 textbook, printed p. 136 (PDF p. 41), Figure 8.2. Trace plant material as it accumulates, is buried and changes over geological time. The drawings simplify a process that varies by location.

figures.heading: Interpret the reservoir cross-section
figures.alt: Textbook cross-section of layered rock with a trapped natural gas layer above oil and water, and wells labelled A to E.
figures.caption: Science 24 textbook, printed p. 140 (PDF p. 45). The full page remains available in Textbook Practice.

figures.heading: From seismic signal to a well
figures.alt: Silhouette of a pump jack at an oil well at sunset; the equipment lifts fluid through a well from below ground.
figures.title: Surface equipment at a well
figures.caption: Science 24 textbook, printed p. 141 (PDF p. 46). This surface pump jack is one possible extraction method; the reservoir lies below the scene.

figures.heading: Trace an infection pathway
figures.alt: Match source, exit, transfer and entry in the infection pathway.
figures.title: Trace an infection pathway
figures.caption: Match source, exit, transfer and entry in the infection pathway. Course diagram for this lesson.

figures.heading: Trace a community water safeguard
figures.alt: Match intake, treatment, monitoring and household delivery.
figures.title: Trace a community water safeguard
figures.caption: Match intake, treatment, monitoring and household delivery. Course diagram for this lesson.

figures.heading: Trace the first two lines of defence
figures.alt: Textbook drawing of a white blood cell leaving a capillary and a macrophage near harmful bacteria in surrounding tissue.
figures.title: Where the response happens
figures.caption: Science 24 textbook, printed p. 195 (PDF p. 32), Figure 11.3. Follow A from the capillary into tissue, then B to the macrophage. This diagram shows a response after a barrier has been crossed.

figures.heading: Trace a targeted immune response
figures.alt: Match the entering antigen, recognition, response and memory.
figures.title: Trace a targeted immune response
figures.caption: Match the entering antigen, recognition, response and memory. Course diagram for this lesson.

figures.heading: Read sequence and chromosome evidence separately
figures.alt: A cell contains a nucleus, a nucleus contains chromosomes, and chromosomes contain DNA. A karyotype shows chromosome number and arrangement, not every DNA base.
figures.title: Keep the three scales separate
figures.caption: Course scale diagram. Inspect all three original karyotypes in workbook pp. 27–28.

figures.heading: Read a Tt × tt cross
figures.alt: Identify parent gametes, the four combinations and the genotype tally.
figures.title: Read a Tt × tt cross
figures.caption: Identify parent gametes, the four combinations and the genotype tally. Course diagram for this lesson.

figures.heading: Read what is drawn before inferring what is hidden
figures.alt: The 2023 workbook pedigree shows Tom and Sue as parents of Sara, Joe and Jim; Jim and Kay have Tim and Lori. Sue, Joe, Jim and Tim are shaded.
figures.title: Read the actual workbook pedigree
figures.caption: Original Science 24 workbook p. 31, question 11. Shading identifies the marked people; it does not supply their genotypes.
